title: Clapham to Adyar: Priest's Wife, Freethinker, Firebrand, President
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Clapham, London, birth
stops.campa: Annie Wood is born in London to William Burton Persse Wood, an underwriter with a scholar's temperament, and Emily Roche Morris, of Irish descent. The comfortable years in St John's Wood end when Annie is five: her father dies of infection caught attending an autopsy, and within months her small brother Alfred follows him to the grave. Emily, left with no settled money, moves the family to relations in Clapham. The girl who will unmake and remake herself seven times over begins in this first, ordinary bereavement.
suggested_refs: Annie Besant, An Autobiography (1893), opening chapters

stops.name: Fern Hill, Charmouth, Dorset: Miss Marryat's schoolroom
stops.campa: Too poor to raise all her children alone, Emily places Annie in the care of Ellen Marryat, sister of the novelist Captain Marryat, at Fern Hill near Charmouth. For five years Annie is drilled in composition, recitation, English, French, later German, and reads without limit in a house that treats a bookish girl as a treasure rather than a problem. She will say the debt is one no words of hers can tell. The love of knowledge fixed here becomes the one constant through every later self she puts on and sheds.
stops.quote: Miss Marryat had a perfect genius for teaching, and took in it the greatest delight... No words of mine can tell how much I owe her, not only of knowledge, but of that love of knowledge which has remained with me ever since as a constant spur to study.
suggested_refs: Fern Hill, Charmouth, Dorset, Ellen Marryat's school

stops.name: St Mary-at-Lambeth, marriage to Frank Besant
stops.campa: At twenty Annie marries Frank Besant, a twenty-seven-year-old Anglican clergyman fresh from Cambridge, a fellow of St Mary Hall, Oxford, and the younger brother of the novelist Walter Besant. She scarcely knows him. Within the marriage she will later set down flatly as an ill-matched pair, she keeps house first at Cheltenham, then bears a son, Arthur Digby, in 1869. She has entered the one identity, clergyman's wife, that she will spend the rest of her life trying to out-argue, out-write, and out-live.
suggested_refs: St Mary-at-Lambeth, where the marriage banns were read

stops.name: Cheltenham, Mabel's fever and the first doubt
stops.campa: Her infant daughter Mabel is seized by whooping cough so violent that more than once she is thought dead already. Annie sits through silent weeks with the dying child on her knees, praying without answer, until she collapses from exhaustion. Out of that vigil grows, in her own words, a feeling of angry resentment against the God she had believed was torturing her helpless baby for weeks on end. Mabel lives. The vicar's wife's faith, quietly, does not.
stops.quote: There had grown up in my mind a feeling of angry resentment against the God who had been for weeks, as I thought, torturing my helpless baby.
suggested_refs: Annie Besant, An Autobiography, the chapter on Mabel's illness
sources: Embryo Project Encyclopedia, Annie Wood Besant

stops.name: Sibsey vicarage, Lincolnshire: the deity of Jesus, denied
stops.campa: Frank Besant takes the living of St Margaret's, Sibsey, in the gift of the Lord Chancellor, and moves his family into the fen-country vicarage. Here, still nominally a clergyman's wife, Annie studies scripture and the Athanasian Creed with the terrible thoroughness she brings to everything, and publishes anonymously a pamphlet denying the deity of Jesus of Nazareth. Money is short, Frank controls what she earns by her pen, and the marriage that was ill-matched from the start begins, in this house, to fail past mending.
suggested_refs: St Margaret's Church, Sibsey, Lincolnshire, Frank Besant's parish 1871-1917

stops.name: Sibsey, refusing the sacrament, and the separation
stops.campa: Unable any longer to profess what she does not believe, Annie refuses to take Communion. Frank, fearing scandal in his own parish, gives her the choice of the altar rail or the door. She chooses the door: expulsion over hypocrisy, she will say of it later. On the twenty-fifth of October the couple sign a legal deed of separation; she takes Mabel to London and a life without pulpit, income, or the protection a clergyman's wife could once claim, and begins to write for her bread.
stops.quote: I was told that I must conform to the outward observances of the Church, and attend the Communion; I refused. Then came the distinct alternative; conformity or exclusion from home — in other words, hypocrisy or expulsion. I chose the latter.
suggested_refs: The deed of separation, 25 October 1873
sources: East End Women's Museum, Annie Besant

segments.name: Bradlaugh and the Fires of Free Thought

stops.name: The Hall of Science, Old Street, hearing Bradlaugh
stops.campa: Separated, penniless of belief, Annie goes to the Hall of Science on Old Street and for the first time hears Charles Bradlaugh speak, the great atheist orator, editor of the National Reformer, president of the National Secular Society. She joins the Society within days. It is the second identity she puts on since Clapham: not clergyman's wife but freethinker, and Bradlaugh, seeing at once what she can do with a platform and a pen, opens both to her.
suggested_refs: The Hall of Science, 142 Old Street, headquarters of the National Secular Society

stops.name: The National Reformer office: Daybreak, and the vice-presidency
stops.campa: Bradlaugh sets her writing a weekly column, Daybreak, for the National Reformer, and within a year she is co-editor and, in time, co-owner of the paper. In 1875 the Society elects her vice-president. She studies physical science at Birkbeck by night, lectures across the country by day, and lives, at last, entirely by her own pen and voice. The vicar's wife who could not be trusted with her own earnings now edits a newspaper that England's respectable classes call blasphemous.
suggested_refs: The National Reformer, weekly organ of the National Secular Society

stops.name: Fleet Street, Fruits of Philosophy delivered to the police
stops.campa: Bradlaugh and Besant resolve to test the Obscene Publications Act head-on. They set up the Freethought Publishing Company, and on the twenty-third of March they carry copies of Charles Knowlton's Fruits of Philosophy, a plain contraceptive manual, already the cause of a bookseller's two years' hard labour in Bristol, to the police, the city solicitor, and the magistrates themselves, announcing they will sell it openly from their own shop. On the fifth of April they are arrested.
suggested_refs: Fruits of Philosophy, or the Private Companion of Young Married People, Charles Knowlton (1832)
sources: National Secular Society, The Fruits of Philosophy trial
Embryo Project Encyclopedia, The Fruits of Philosophy

stops.name: Westminster Hall, the trial before Lord Chief Justice Cockburn
stops.campa: The Crown brings Bradlaugh and Besant before the Court of Queen's Bench at Westminster Hall, Lord Chief Justice Cockburn presiding, while some twenty thousand supporters crowd the streets outside. For four days the case for birth control for the poor is argued in open court, a subject respectable London will not speak above a whisper. The jury returns a divided, qualified verdict of guilty; sentence is passed and stayed pending appeal. The book itself will go on to sell two hundred thousand copies before the decade is out.
suggested_refs: Bradlaugh v. The Queen (1877), Court of Queen's Bench
sources: Econlib, The Trial of Annie Besant and Charles Bradlaugh
National Secular Society, The Fruits of Philosophy trial

stops.name: The Rolls Court, Chancery Lane, losing Mabel and Digby
stops.campa: The conviction is quashed the next year on a technicality in the indictment's wording, a hollow victory. Frank Besant, citing her atheism and her authorship of the frank pamphlet The Law of Population, goes to court and wins: the law finds her an unfit mother and strips her of both children. Digby is already living with his father; now Mabel is taken too. She will call it the heaviest blow of her secularist years, heavier than prison would have been.
suggested_refs: The Law of Population, Annie Besant (1878)
sources: Gareth Stedman Jones, 'The Flight of a Clergyman's Wife', LRB

segments.name: The Match Girls and the New Unionism

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, Bloody Sunday
stops.campa: Police baton-charge an unemployed workers' demonstration in Trafalgar Square, killing at least one man on what London will remember as Bloody Sunday. Annie, by now the platform's most fearless woman, walks into the square and offers herself for arrest alongside the crowd rather than stand apart from it. She is by this point as much a socialist as a secularist, drawn by Bradlaugh's old rival Hyndman's Marxism and by the Fabians alike toward the labouring poor whose conditions she has only begun to document.
suggested_refs: Trafalgar Square, site of the 1887 'Bloody Sunday' demonstration

stops.name: Bow: Bryant & May, and White Slavery in London
stops.campa: Annie visits the match-workers of Bryant & May in Bow and hears how fourteen-hour days are paid a starvation wage further docked by fines for dropped matches or a trip to the lavatory, while phosphorus rots the girls' jaws. In her paper The Link she publishes White Slavery in London, naming the shareholders' profits against the workers' poverty. Two girls tell her plainly it is time someone came and helped; she resolves, unlike so many who wish a cause well, to risk something for it herself.
stops.quote: It is time some one came and helped us... Who will help? Plenty of people wish well to any good cause; but very few care to exert themselves to help it, and still fewer will risk anything in its support.
stops.quote_source: Annie Besant, An Autobiography (1893), recalling the match girls of 1888
suggested_refs: The Link, Annie Besant's weekly paper
The Bryant & May match factory, Fairfield Road, Bow

stops.name: Bow, the Union of Women Match Makers, and the settlement
stops.campa: Bryant & May's management, enraged, tries to force the workforce to sign a denial and sacks those they suspect of talking to the press. Some fourteen hundred women and girls walk out. Annie raises strike funds, organises relief, and helps found the Union of Women Match Makers, one of the first unions of women workers in Britain. By the sixteenth of July the fines, the docked wages, and the phosphorus-tainted mess-room are abolished; the match girls have won, and unskilled women's unionism has its first great victory.
suggested_refs: The Union of Women Match Makers, founded 1888
sources: The National Archives, The 1888 matchgirls' strike
People's History Museum, The Match Girls' Strike

stops.name: Tower Hamlets, elected to the London School Board
stops.campa: On the strength of the match girls' victory and years on secularist and socialist platforms, Annie stands for the London School Board and tops the poll in Tower Hamlets with more than fifteen thousand votes, the largest of any candidate in England that year. Denied her own children by a court that called her unfit, she now sits in office over the education of London's poorest, free dinners, free boots, medical inspection, turning private grief into a public office she can actually wield.
suggested_refs: The London School Board, Tower Hamlets division
sources: East End Women's Museum, Annie Besant

stops.name: St James's Hall, the debate with Hyndman
stops.campa: Bradlaugh and the Marxist Henry Hyndman debate socialism versus individualism before a packed St James's Hall, and Annie, still Bradlaugh's ally on the secularist platform, watches the argument that will pull her toward socialism turn public and sharp. Within a year she will join the Fabian Society that Hyndman's rivals are founding, carrying into it the oratory she has spent a decade sharpening in halls just like this one, against opponents just as formidable.
suggested_refs: St James's Hall, Piccadilly, site of the 1884 socialism debate

stops.name: London, recruited to the Fabian Society by Shaw
stops.campa: George Bernard Shaw, twenty-eight and already certain of her gifts, recruits Annie into the young Fabian Society, calling it a triumph to have gained the woman he names the greatest orator in England. She lectures, writes, and organises for the Fabians as she once did for the secularists, and a friendship with Shaw takes root that will survive nearly every later change of her convictions, even the one that costs him her company as a fellow socialist.
stops.quote_source: George Bernard Shaw, on recruiting Besant to the Fabian Society, 1885
suggested_refs: Fabian Society meeting rooms, London, 1880s

stops.name: London: Fabian Essays, and the lapsing socialist
stops.campa: Fabian Essays in Socialism appears at the end of 1889 with Annie's chapter, Industry Under Socialism, alongside Shaw's, Webb's, and Olivier's, twenty-seven thousand copies in two years, a landmark of English socialism. But by the time it is in the shops she has already met Blavatsky and joined the Theosophical Society; within a year she lets her Fabian membership lapse and breaks with the Marxists. Shaw and the others are stunned. She has changed convictions whole before, and will again.
suggested_refs: Fabian Essays in Socialism, ed. G. Bernard Shaw (1889)

stops.name: London: Walter Scott's cheap edition
stops.date_confidence: 1890 for the Walter Scott Publishing Co.'s cheap edition of Fabian Essays in Socialism, confirmed via an AbeBooks bibliographic listing (cover by Walter Crane, cloth boards, publisher's advertisements bound in); no month given, day defaults to 01. The same firm's 1896 edition of Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward is confirmed via ISFDB Publication Record #84911.
stops.campa: Within a year of the Fabian Society's own first printing, the Walter Scott Publishing Co. issues its own cheap edition of Fabian Essays, cover by Walter Crane, cloth boards, publisher's advertisements bound into the back, carrying Annie's chapter to a wider and cheaper readership than the original run reached. The same London firm will publish its own edition of Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward in 1896, his novel of a man asleep for a century sold eventually from the same list as her committees and gradual change.
suggested_refs: Fabian Essays in Socialism, Walter Scott Publishing Co. cheap edition, London, 1890 (AbeBooks listing 9865946548)
Looking Backward (2000-1887), Walter Scott, London, 1896 (ISFDB Publication Record #84911)
sources: AbeBooks bibliographic listing for Fabian Essays in Socialism, Walter Scott Publishing Co., 1890 (verified)
ISFDB Publication Record #84911, Looking Backward, Walter Scott, 1896 (verified)

segments.name: The Secret Doctrine, and the Overnight Conversion

stops.name: London, reviewing The Secret Doctrine for the Pall Mall Gazette
stops.campa: Asked to review Helena Blavatsky's vast, difficult Secret Doctrine for the Pall Mall Gazette, Annie sits with a book most reviewers would refuse outright and finds in it not nonsense but a rock, she writes, whence every faith's disjointed fragments were hewn. She will not simply endorse it and will not dismiss it either: all who keep an open door to truth, she concludes, will give scrutiny to any visitant, be the garb of Asia or of Europe. The door, once opened, does not close again.
stops.quote: All who keep an open door to Truth will give scrutiny to any visitant, be the garb of Asia or of Europe, be the tongue of Paris or of Ind.
stops.quote_source: Annie Besant, review of The Secret Doctrine, Pall Mall Gazette, 1889
suggested_refs: H.P. Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine (1888)
sources: blavatskyarchives.com, Among the Adepts: Besant on The Secret Doctrine

stops.name: 17 Lansdowne Road, meeting Blavatsky
stops.campa: On the evening of the tenth of May, with her friend Herbert Burrows, Annie calls at 17 Lansdowne Road, Holland Park, where Helena Blavatsky keeps her London lodgings and the Blavatsky Lodge meets. The old Russian is exactly as strange as report has made her, and exactly as commanding. Before the evening ends Blavatsky has told Annie plainly that she wants her in the Society. Annie, freethinker of fifteen years, feels something in the room she has no vocabulary yet to name.
suggested_refs: 17 Lansdowne Road, Holland Park, HPB's London residence
sources: Theosophical Society in America, Esoteric World Chapter 22

stops.name: 17 Lansdowne Road, joining the Theosophical Society
stops.campa: Eleven days after the meeting, Annie signs her name into the Theosophical Society. London's secularists and socialists alike are thunderstruck: the great materialist orator, kneeling, as they see it, to Asiatic mysticism and an old woman's cosmology of root-races and rounds. She will spend the rest of her life mapping the same clarity of purpose she brought to Bradlaugh's platform onto Blavatsky's cosmos, and will never again change her convictions this completely.
suggested_refs: The Theosophical Society membership roll, London, 21 May 1889

stops.name: Hall of Science, Why I Became a Theosophist
stops.campa: In the same Hall of Science where she first heard Bradlaugh fifteen years before, Annie now delivers the lecture Why I Became a Theosophist to the freethinkers who once claimed her as their own. She does not renounce the reasoning that carried her through secularism, birth control, and the picket line; she says only that Theosophy answers questions materialism left open. It is a fourth identity worn over the same restless hunger for a truth that will finally hold still.
suggested_refs: 'Why I Became a Theosophist', lecture, Hall of Science, 4 and 11 August 1889
sources: Theosophical Society in America, Esoteric World

stops.name: 19 Avenue Road, Blavatsky's deathbed: 'Keep the link unbroken'
stops.campa: Influenza scythes through London and takes Blavatsky at 19 Avenue Road on the eighth of May. Two nights before, she had charged the disciples at her side with the whole burden of the future: keep the link unbroken, do not let my last incarnation be a failure. Annie is among those at the bedside. Her body is burned at Woking; the ashes are divided between New York, London, and Adyar. Annie, forty-three and only two years a Theosophist, becomes overnight the movement's most capable voice.
stops.quote: Keep the link unbroken! Do not let my last incarnation be a failure.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, last message to the Esoteric School, recorded by those present, 6 May 1891
suggested_refs: 19 Avenue Road, St John's Wood
White Lotus Day
Woking Crematorium

stops.name: Adyar, first landing in India
stops.campa: Four years a Theosophist, Annie sails for India for the first time to attend the Society's annual Convention at Adyar, the compound on the river outside Madras that Blavatsky and Olcott made the movement's world headquarters under its great banyan. She arrives already fluent in the doctrine and already loved by Indians who see in a white woman's reverence for their own philosophy something the Raj has rarely offered. Adyar, from this landing on, will be more truly her home than London ever was again.
suggested_refs: Adyar, Theosophical Society international headquarters, Madras

stops.name: Benares, founding the Central Hindu College
stops.campa: In a rented house at Karnaghanta, Annie and the English science graduate Arthur Richardson open the Central Hindu College, teaching modern science beside Hindu scripture and ritual to counter what she calls the denigration of India's own culture by government schools. It is the seed of Banaras Hindu University, which will grow from it in 1916. She will later hand its administration to Madan Mohan Malviya, but the college is hers first: proof that a foreigner's reverence can build rather than only borrow.
suggested_refs: Central Hindu College, Benares (now Varanasi), founded 1898

stops.name: Adyar, elected President of the Theosophical Society
stops.campa: Henry Steel Olcott, co-founder and first president, dies at Adyar in February; some members claim the Masters themselves named Annie his successor at his deathbed, a claim disputed even within the Society. She stands instead for election as the rules require, and the membership returns her by a landslide, 9,572 votes to 1,089. She will be re-elected for successive seven-year terms until she dies, the vicar's discarded wife now head of a Society with lodges on every continent.
suggested_refs: The Theosophical Society presidential election, 1907

stops.name: Adyar beach, Leadbeater finds the boy
stops.campa: Walking the private beach below the Adyar compound, Charles Webster Leadbeater notices a thin, sickly fourteen-year-old, Jiddu Krishnamurti, living there with his father and brother, and is struck by an aura he declares more radiant than any he has seen. He tells Annie at once. When she returns to Adyar she looks at the boy herself and feels, she will say, the same unmistakable intuition: that this is the vehicle long awaited for the coming World Teacher. Nothing in her remaining years will matter more than what she does next.
suggested_refs: The Adyar river beach, Theosophical Society compound
C. W. Leadbeater's account of the discovery

segments.name: The Order of the Star, and the Break with Steiner

stops.name: Adyar, legal guardian of the Krishnamurti brothers
stops.campa: Annie admits Krishnamurti and his brother Nityananda into the Society and its inner Esoteric Section, and in March becomes their legal guardian, over their father's later bitter objection and eventual lawsuit. The boys are taken from ordinary Indian family life into the Theosophical compound, tutored in English manners and European languages, and groomed for a role neither of them asked for. Annie's devotion to the project is total and, in the fullest sense of the word, maternal.
suggested_refs: The guardianship suit, Narayaniah v. Besant

stops.name: Benares, the Order of the Star in the East founded
stops.campa: Annie founds the Order of the Star in the East, an international body drawing together all who await a coming World Teacher, and names the sixteen-year-old Krishnamurti its Head, with herself and Leadbeater as its Protectors. The Order gathers up, its charter says, the common expectation of every faith into a single movement of preparation. Thousands join within months. She has built, in effect, a church around a boy she loves and a prophecy she has staked her presidency on.
stops.quote: To gather up and unify this common expectation, wherever and in whatever form it may exist, and to link it into a single great movement of preparation for the Great One whom the age awaits.
stops.quote_source: Founding statement, Order of the Star in the East, 1911
suggested_refs: Founding documents of the Order of the Star in the East, 1911
sources: Wikipedia, Order of the Star in the East
Theosophy Wiki, Order of the Star in the East

stops.name: Adyar, word arrives that Steiner has refused
stops.campa: From Berlin comes Rudolf Steiner's flat refusal of the Order: Christ, he holds, came once in the flesh and comes now only in the etheric, and no committee may incarnate him twice. He declares Star membership incompatible with membership in his own German Section. Annie, who has staked the Society's unity on the Order's reception, will not let a section defy Adyar's charter. She answers refusal with authority: within weeks she moves to strike the German Section's charter altogether.
suggested_refs: Rudolf Steiner's public refusal of the Order of the Star, December 1912
steiner.journey.json (the schism, cross-referenced)
sources: Rudolf Steiner Archive, GA250, History of the German Section

stops.name: Adyar, the German Section's charter revoked
stops.campa: On the seventh of March, from Adyar, Annie revokes the charter of the German Section for its refusal to admit members of the Order of the Star in the East, the formal act that severs Steiner and the great majority of German-speaking Theosophists from the Society she leads. Steiner, who had already founded his Anthroposophical Society at Cologne at the end of December, loses nothing he has not already walked away from; Annie loses a section that took ten years to build and will not return.
suggested_refs: The revocation of the German Section charter, 7 March 1913
sources: Wikipedia, Rudolf Steiner and the Theosophical Society

segments.name: Home Rule, and the Congress Presidency

stops.name: Madras: New India, a daily for Home Rule
stops.campa: As the war in Europe opens, Annie founds and edits the daily New India in Madras, turning the same editorial weapon she once wielded for Bradlaugh's freethought onto the cause of Indian self-government. Her articles argue, week after week, that a people fit to fight and die for the Empire in Flanders and Mesopotamia is fit to govern its own affairs at home. The colonial government watches her with the particular unease it reserves for a Englishwoman turned against it from inside its own institutions.
suggested_refs: New India, Annie Besant's daily newspaper, Madras

stops.name: Bombay, the All India Home Rule League
stops.campa: Annie, in step with Bal Gangadhar Tilak's twin league launched that April, founds the All India Home Rule League, modelled openly on the Irish precedent, demanding self-government within the Empire on a fixed and public timetable rather than the Congress's older, gentler petitioning. She tours the country lecturing to crowds that have never before been addressed in these terms by anyone, let alone a European woman, and the League's branches multiply through 1916 and 1917 into the first true mass nationalist organisation India has had.
suggested_refs: The All India Home Rule League, founded 1916

stops.name: Ootacamund, arrest and internment
stops.campa: The government orders Annie and her lieutenants B. P. Wadia and George Arundale arrested for their Home Rule agitation; she chooses internment at Ootacamund in the Nilgiri hills, at the Society's own twin bungalows, Olcott Cottage and Gulistan. Confined for ninety-three days, she has a red-and-green Home Rule flag run up over the bungalow each night for her supporters below to salute. The arrest, meant to silence her, makes her instead the single most famous name in Indian nationalism.
suggested_refs: Olcott Cottage and Gulistan, Ootacamund
The Home Rule flag, designed by Annie Besant
sources: Nehru Archive, The Internment of Mrs. Annie Besant
Deccan Chronicle, Annie Besant's house arrest in Ooty

stops.name: Ootacamund, released to a nation's welcome
stops.campa: The government relents in September and releases the three internees. Annie travels from town to town on her way back toward Madras through crowds that gather at every station to garland and cheer her; the internment that was meant to break the Home Rule agitation has instead made her, by the government's own officials' admission, the most popular figure in the country. She arrives at the height of a fame no Englishwoman before or since will hold in India.
suggested_refs: The nationwide welcome tour, September 1917
sources: Nilgiri Discovery Centre, Dr. Annie Besant

stops.name: Calcutta, President of the Indian National Congress
stops.campa: At the thirty-second session of the Indian National Congress, Annie is installed as its president, the first woman, and the first person of British birth, to hold the office. Her presidential address, published as The Case for India, reviews the war's toll on Indian soldiers, honours the recently dead Dadabhai Naoroji, and insists that freedom is the birthright of every nation, self-government the due of any people proud enough to demand it. The vicar's runaway wife now speaks for a subcontinent.
stops.quote: Freedom is the birthright of every nation.
stops.quote_source: Annie Besant, presidential address, Indian National Congress, Calcutta, 26 December 1917 ('The Case for India')
suggested_refs: The Case for India, presidential address, Calcutta, 26 December 1917
sources: Internet Archive, The Case for India

segments.name: The Dissolution, and Adyar's Last Years

stops.name: Ommen, the Netherlands: the Order dissolved before her
stops.campa: At the Star Camp at Ommen, before some three thousand members and Annie herself, Krishnamurti stands and dissolves the Order of the Star in the East, the body built entirely around him, declaring truth a pathless land no organisation, sect, or teacher can lead anyone toward. Annie, eighty-two, watches twenty years of devotion: legal guardianship, a movement, a doctrine, her own presidency's central purpose, unmade in a single afternoon by the boy she raised to speak exactly this freely. She does not fight him.
stops.quote: I maintain that Truth is a pathless land, and you cannot approach it by any path whatsoever, by any religion, by any sect.
stops.quote_source: Jiddu Krishnamurti, dissolution speech, Ommen, 3 August 1929
suggested_refs: The Ommen Star Camp grounds, the Netherlands
Krishnamurti's dissolution speech, 3 August 1929
sources: Krishnamurti Foundation, Order of the Star Dissolution Speech
Wikipedia, Order of the Star in the East

stops.name: Adyar, reopening the Esoteric Section, alone
stops.campa: The year before the dissolution, in sympathy with Krishnamurti's growing unease, Annie had closed the Society's inner Esoteric Section outright; now, after Ommen, she reopens it without him, and without the prophecy that had organised her last two decades. She keeps the presidency, keeps Adyar, keeps writing and lecturing into her eighties, but the great structure of expectation she raised around a boy found on a beach has come down, and she is the only one left standing amid it.
suggested_refs: The Esoteric Section of the Theosophical Society
sources: Quora, Besant's reaction to the dissolution
Theosophy Wiki, Order of the Star in the East

stops.name: Adyar, the last public work, failing health
stops.campa: Past eighty and increasingly frail, Annie still presides over Convention, still corresponds across the Society's lodges on every continent, still speaks for Indian self-rule when her strength allows it. The illnesses of old age now overtake a body that spent sixty years addressing crowds in halls, courtrooms, prison yards, and internment bungalows without pause. Adyar's staff and her old comrades, Arundale, Wadia, the Krishnamurti brothers themselves, reconciled if not restored, gather increasingly around her chair rather than her platform.
suggested_refs: Annie Besant's final years at Adyar, 1930-1933
sources: Kamat's Potpourri, Biography of Annie Besant

stops.name: Adyar, death
stops.campa: Annie dies at Adyar on the afternoon of the twentieth of September, eighty-five years old, President of the Theosophical Society for twenty-six unbroken years. Her body is cremated on the grounds where she found Krishnamurti on the beach and buried a schism with Steiner in a single revoked charter; Charles Leadbeater, her old collaborator, lights the pyre. She has been, in successive whole lives, a priest's wife, an atheist, a birth-control convict, a unionist, a Fabian, a Theosophist, and a nation's president, and dies still all of them at once.
suggested_refs: The cremation ground, Theosophical Society estate, Adyar
sources: Theosophy Wiki, Garden of Remembrance at Adyar

stops.name: Benares, the ashes given to the Ganga
stops.campa: A portion of Annie's ashes travels to Benares, carried by Bhagavan Das in a great procession to the river, and is given to the waters of the Ganga on the first of October, her eighty-sixth birthday, had she lived to see it. The rest remains at Adyar's Garden of Remembrance, on the ground of the cremation itself. The freethinker who once denied every god by name ends her ashes in a river India calls holy, given there by the very students her Central Hindu College first gathered.
suggested_refs: The Ganga at Benares, where a portion of her ashes was committed
